[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §5.6; Title Commitment Schedule B, Part II, Exceptions 1–7; Requirements 3, 4, 9.
[P]The term sheet requires the title policy to insure Lender's first-priority lien "subject only to those exceptions approved by Lender in writing ('Permitted Exceptions')" — but there is nothing in the file showing that approval. I have drafted **Exhibit B** from Schedule B, Part II, with an express condition that no matter not listed has been approved, and a conditions-to-approval paragraph requiring the endorsements listed in Section 5.6 of the term sheet (zoning, access, survey, comprehensive and future advance) plus, on my recommendation, contiguity, subdivision and ALTA 28.1 encroachment coverage.
[P]The **future advance endorsement** deserves emphasis. The Renovation Holdback is $2,250,000 advanced over fourteen months after recording, during which time mechanics' and materialmen's liens will arise. The Mortgage states that the holdback advances are intended to have the same priority as the Initial Advance (Section 2.5), but that intention is only as good as the title coverage behind it. Confirm the endorsement covers obligatory advances and that the Bank's disbursement obligations are, in fact, obligatory and not discretionary in the loan documents — the endorsement will follow the documents, not our hopes. Section 9.4 conditions each advance but does not give Lender a free refusal right other than on default; that is deliberate, and it should be preserved.
[P]I have also listed the land use restriction (Exception 4) as a Permitted Exception with an express statement that it "may not be removed," since the title company has said as much, and cross-referenced Article VIII so that the Bank's approval of the exception is not read as a waiver of the compliance covenants (Section 2.7 says this expressly).
[H]**Issue 12 — The balcony encroachment has no permit or license in the record.**
[1]**Source:** Title Commitment, Schedule B-II, Exception 5 and Notes to Closer ¶2; Appraisal §2.1 and §5; Renovation Budget, line item 3.
[P]A decorative iron balcony extends approximately 2.5 feet over the King Street right-of-way. The title company makes no representation about any permit, license or encroachment agreement, recommends ALTA 28.1 if coverage is wanted, and the appraiser (who treats the encroachment as immaterial to value) nevertheless recommends the Bank confirm a valid permit. There is none in the file. Two further points: the renovation budget includes $625,000 of façade restoration of which the balcony repair is a component, so the Bank will be funding work on the encroaching structure; and Borrower is not permitted to remove or alter it without consent under Section 7.7. I have drafted a representation that no encroachment agreement has been obtained and no notice requiring removal has been received (Section 5.5), added the ALTA 28.1 endorsement to the Exhibit B conditions, and required evidence of any license (or the Bank's written acknowledgment that none exists) as a condition of approving the exception. If the City later requires removal, the façade scope increases beyond the budget — a cost overrun that Section 9.7 puts on Borrower, but which the Completion Guaranty should be read to cover.
[H]**Issue 13 — Sources and uses do not fund closing costs, the TI/LC reserve or leasing commissions.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §§3.3, 3.4, 6.3, 8.2, 13.1, 13.2; Exhibit B to the Term Sheet; Rent Roll workbook, "Vacancy Schedule" tab; your markup notes, Section 6.
[P]Total Project Cost is $20,950,000 ($17,800,000 purchase price plus $3,150,000 renovation). Sources are the $14,750,000 Loan and Borrower equity of $6,200,000, and those figures reconcile exactly. But Borrower's equity is fully spoken for: $5,300,000 is the gap between the purchase price and the $12,500,000 Initial Advance, and $900,000 is the renovation equity required by Exhibit B to the term sheet. That leaves nothing for:
[T]
[R]Unfunded use | Amount | Source
[R]Loan origination fee (1.00%) | $147,500 | Term Sheet §13.1
[R]Documentary stamp tax on the Mortgage (0.37%, subject to confirmation — see Issue 20) | $54,575 | Your markup notes, Section 6
[R]Tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve funded at closing | $150,000 | Term Sheet §6.3
[R]Leasing commissions projected for Bay 2 and Suite B ($28,500 + $61,250) | $89,750 | Rent Roll workbook, "Vacancy Schedule" tab
[R]**Subtotal of identified unfunded uses** | **$441,825** | 
[P]Title premiums, the ALTA survey, appraisal, Phase I, and Lender's legal fees under Section 13.2 of the term sheet would add to that figure. The Bank should see an updated sources and uses statement before closing. Note the interaction with the negative covenants: Borrower cannot close the gap with additional borrowing (Section 7.1), so either the equity commitment increases above $6,200,000 or the Bank funds/closes some of these items. I have drafted the reserve funding obligation (Section 10.3, $150,000 at closing) and the expense obligations (Section 14.9) as absolute, without acknowledging that the funding source does not exist — that is a question for the Bank.
[H]**Issue 14 — The two reserve and allowance mechanisms overlap, and the draw schedule does not implement the retainage the term sheet requires.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §§6.3, 8.2, 8.4; Renovation Budget workbook, both tabs; your markup notes, Section 6.
[P]Two funding sources cover the same costs: the Renovation Budget carries $550,000 of tenant improvement allowances ($450,000 from the holdback, $100,000 from equity), and the term sheet separately requires a $150,000 tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve at closing. Nothing in the record says which pays what, and the $150,000 reserve is subject to a replenishment obligation within 30 days of each draw, which is a recurring cash drain. I have drafted Section 10.3 to prohibit use of the reserve for any cost included in the Renovation Budget "except to the extent Lender approves in writing an allocation between the two sources of funds," and Section 9.2 to prohibit reallocation among budget line items without consent. That forces the Bank to make the allocation at the first draw rather than after the fact, but the Bank should approve a written funding protocol now. Note also that the leasing commissions ($89,750 in the vacancy schedule) appear in no budget at all.
[P]On retainage: term sheet Section 8.4 requires 10% retainage from each disbursement of the holdback until substantial completion. The draw schedule workbook does not apply retainage — it draws the holdback to zero by month 14 on a gross basis. Section 9.5 imposes retainage as a matter of the Mortgage, and Section 9.6 releases it on the conditions stated. Borrower's architect and the Bank's inspector should re-cast the draw schedule to show net-of-retainage draws, or the holdback will be exhausted before the work is complete and Borrower will be funding the last 10% out of pocket without having planned for it.
[A]VI. FIGURES: WHAT I RECOMPUTED AND WHAT DID NOT RECONCILE
[P]Every figure in the Mortgage was recomputed. The full reconciliation is Appendix A. The items that matter for the draft or for the Bank's file are these.
[H]**Issue 15 — In-place rent of $415,100 is stale; two of the three leases have already escalated.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §2.3; Rent Roll workbook, "Summary" and "Lease Abstracts" tabs.
[P]$415,100 is arithmetically correct as 3,800 × $28.50 + 3,800 × $24.00 + 9,800 × $22.00. The problem is that those are the original contract rates, not the current rates. The Lowcountry Provisions lease escalates 3% each January 1 beginning January 1, 2025, so the rate in effect at an April 2025 closing is $29.355/SF ($111,549 per year), not $28.50 ($108,300); the rent roll's own escalation schedule says exactly that. The Harmon & Wren lease escalates 2.5% each July 1 beginning July 1, 2023, so the rate in effect is $25.215/SF ($95,817 per year), not $24.00 ($91,200) — and again the rent roll's schedule says so while the "Current Base Rent" line does not. The rent roll is internally inconsistent, and the "current" figures understate in-place rent by $7,866 per year (1.9%). Tidemark's escalation does not begin until April 1, 2026, so $215,600 is correct.
[P]This cuts in the borrower's favor on NOI and therefore against the Bank on DSCR and appraised value, so I would rather the Bank discover it from us than from borrower's counsel. I have not represented the $415,100 figure as current: Exhibit D states the base rents "as delivered to Lender" and requires Borrower to certify the escalated rents in effect on each reporting date (Section 6.6), and Exhibit D recites the escalation provisions in full.
[H]**Issue 16 — The draw schedule contains two arithmetic errors and a line-item misallocation.**
[1]**Source:** Renovation Budget and Draw Schedule workbook, "Draw Schedule" tab.
[P]Three defects, none large but all indicative of a schedule prepared without a cross-check: (i) Borrower equity across the fourteen draws totals **$905,000** against a commitment of $900,000 — the final row shows remaining equity of negative $5,000, and total combined draws of $3,155,000 against a budget of $3,150,000; (ii) the HVAC line draws **$1,250,000** ($900,000 from the holdback plus $350,000 from equity) against a budget of $1,200,000, while the elevator line draws $425,000 against a budget of $475,000 — a $50,000 shift between line items that the Budget Detail tab does not authorize; and (iii) as noted in Issue 14, no retainage. I have drafted Section 9.2 to prohibit draws in excess of a line item's allocation, which would stop defect (ii) at the first draw, and Section 9.4(d) to condition each advance on remaining availability. The schedule should be corrected and re-certified before it is used as the disbursement protocol.
[H]**Issue 17 — The DSCR test date differs across the file by nearly three months.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §7.1; your markup notes, Section 6; Rent Roll workbook, "Summary" and "Vacancy Schedule" tabs.
[P]The term sheet says the first test date is "the first full calendar quarter ending after the twenty-fourth month following closing (anticipated to be approximately July 15, 2027, for the quarter ending June 30, 2027)." Your notes say April 15, 2027. The rent roll summary says April 15, 2027, and the vacancy schedule assumes all spaces leased by April 15, 2027. The term sheet governs, and I have drafted July 15, 2027 for the quarter ending June 30, 2027 (Section 6.5(a)). The difference is not cosmetic: on the vacancy schedule, Suite B's rent commencement is projected for February 1, 2027, leaving 2.5 months of rent before an April test date and 5 months before a July test date. The Bank's lease-up expectations should be expressed against the correct date.

[R]Unfunded use | Amount | Source
[R]Loan origination fee (1.00%) | $147,500 | Term Sheet §13.1
[R]Documentary stamp tax on the Mortgage (0.37%, subject to confirmation — see Issue 20) | $54,575 | Your markup notes, Section 6
[R]Tenant improvement and leasing commission reserve funded at closing | $150,000 | Term Sheet §6.3
[R]Leasing commissions projected for Bay 2 and Suite B ($28,500 + $61,250) | $89,750 | Rent Roll workbook, "Vacancy Schedule" tab
[R]**Subtotal of identified unfunded uses** | **$441,825** |

[H]**Issue 15 — In-place rent of $415,100 is stale; two of the three leases have already escalated.**

[P]The operating agreement summary confirms each of your concerns and adds one. (i) The purpose clause is limited to the Property but ends with "any and all activities necessary, incidental, or related thereto," and the summary states affirmatively that the agreement "does not contain any language restricting the Company to single-purpose entity status." (ii) There are no separateness covenants. (iii) There is no independent director or independent manager, no springing member, and no provision requiring any independent consent to a bankruptcy filing; the summary says so in terms. (iv) The term is perpetual and there is no lender consent requirement for dissolution, merger or amendment. (v) The additional point: the Major Decisions list requires 75% member approval for financing above $1,000,000, so this Loan required member approval (see Issue 20) — and voluntary bankruptcy is *not* on the Major Decisions list, which means the managing member alone could file. [P]Term sheet Section 10.1(g) requires Borrower's organizational documents to be amended, to the extent necessary, to include these restrictions "prior to closing." I have not done that, for three reasons. First, we know the representation would be false when made; a false representation in a document the Bank relies on is not a drafting technique, it is a misrepresentation, and it would be a poor foundation for the Bank's file if the loan later goes bad. Second, a knowingly false representation of SPE status would itself be a fraud carve-out event under Section 14.15(a) — we would be manufacturing the very recourse trigger the SPE structure is supposed to make remote. Third, the representation protects the Bank, and a representation we know to be untrue protects no one.
[P]What I have done instead: Section 5.7 represents that Borrower "is and shall be" a Single-Purpose Entity "on and as of the Closing Date, and after giving effect to the Operating Agreement Amendment delivered at Closing"; Section 6.8 obliges Borrower to deliver the amendment, executed by all three members, together with the good standing certificate, incumbency certificate and member resolutions; and Article XII/12.1(h) makes any failure to maintain the organizational provisions of Section 6.8 an Event of Default without cure. [H]**Issue 22 — The Harmon & Wren lease carries a right of first refusal on Bay 2, a near-term expiration and a termination right whose exercise deadline has passed.**
[1]**Source:** Rent Roll workbook, "Lease Abstracts" tab; Appraisal §§3.2, 6.3.
[P]Three features of this lease bear on the leasing covenant and on the Bank's lease-up math. (i) Harmon & Wren holds a right of first refusal on Bay 2, exercisable within 15 business days of any bona fide third-party offer, surviving renewal of its own lease; the appraiser concludes it will add 60–90 days to the Bay 2 absorption period. Section 6.4(a) therefore requires Borrower to comply with the ROFR before executing any lease of Bay 2 or entering any exclusive negotiation, and Section 6.4(b) applies the consent threshold to new leases and to amendments and renewals. The interaction is worth flagging to the Bank: because a renewal of Harmon & Wren's lease is itself an instrument that could be drafted to extend the ROFR, Section 6.4(b)'s consent requirement should be applied to any renewal that is not on the terms described in Exhibit D. (ii) The lease expires June 30, 2026, with a renewal notice deadline of December 31, 2025 — four months before this loan's estimated closing and inside the loan term. If the tenant does not renew, Bay 3 becomes vacant in the same period the Bank expects Suite B to lease, and the vacancy schedule flags that scenario as compounding the lease-up problem. (iii) The abstract recites an early termination right effective June 30, 2025 on payment of three months' rent with six months' prior notice; the notice deadline of December 31, 2024 has passed without exercise. Confirm in writing at closing that the right has lapsed, and obtain it in the estoppel.
[H]**Issue 23 — The leases' subordination provisions are inconsistent, and the Lowcountry lease has none.**
[1]**Source:** Rent Roll workbook, "Lease Abstracts" tab; Title Commitment Schedule B-II, Exception 6.
[P]Harmon & Wren and Tidemark both subordinate to future mortgages — Harmon & Wren conditionally on delivery of a commercially reasonable non-disturbance agreement, which means the Bank must be prepared to give one on terms the tenant will accept. Lowcountry has no subordination at all. The practical effect is that the Bank's lien will be prior to the leases as a matter of recording law, but its ability to deliver the SNDAs the term sheet makes conditions precedent (Section 12.1(k)) depends on three separate tenant negotiations, one of which has no contractual starting point. I recommend the Bank's form of SNDA be circulated to all three tenants before closing and that the form be reviewed against Harmon & Wren's "commercially reasonable" standard rather than presented cold.
[A]VII. ENVIRONMENTAL — THE SCDHEC LAND USE RESTRICTION
[H]**Issue 24 — The land use restriction is a permanent title matter with continuing affirmative obligations, and the draft makes it a stand-alone covenant structure.**
[1]**Source:** Phase I ESA §§5.1–5.4 and 6(d); Title Commitment Schedule B-II, Exception 4 and Notes to Closer ¶1; Term Sheet §5.4.
[P]The Phase I identifies one Controlled Recognized Environmental Condition: PCE and petroleum solvent contamination from the former dry cleaning operation at 518 King Street (off-site) migrating into the southwest corner of Lot 7, remediated under SCDHEC oversight, closed by a No Further Action letter dated August 12, 2021 (SCDHEC Site ID SC-29403-0772), and controlled by a land use restriction recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89 that (a) prohibits residential use of the ground floor of Lot 7 (Bay 1, 3,800 SF) and (b) requires that the vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 slab be maintained and periodically inspected. The restriction runs with the land, cannot be removed without SCDHEC approval, and the No Further Action status is contingent on continued compliance. The Bank waived the Phase II requirement in correspondence dated January 22, 2025.
[P]Both the title commitment (Special Instruction 1) and the Phase I (recommendation 6(d)) require the loan documents to address this specifically. Article VIII does: Section 8.2 recites the restriction and prohibits any violation, modification, termination or release without Lender's consent; Section 8.3 imposes the vapor barrier obligations, including written notice to the contractor, SCDHEC notification before any work affecting the slab, and delivery of a licensed professional's certification of integrity on request; Section 8.4 prohibits residential use of the ground floor of Lot 7 and requires a conforming covenant in every lease of that space; Section 8.6 prohibits seeking amendment or termination; and Section 12.3 makes any breach an immediate Event of Default without cure. Section 5.9 contains the corresponding representations.
[P]Two things to note. First, this is drafted as an immediate default with no cure, at the title company's suggestion and consistent with the term sheet's "bad boy" structure for environmental matters — but a vapor barrier breach may be curable by repair, and Borrower's counsel will likely ask for a cure period confined to defaults curable solely by repair and inspection. I would resist a general cure right but consider a narrow one. Second, the Bank should require the pre-acquisition vapor barrier inspection the Phase I recommends (recommendation (b)) as a closing condition. **It is not a term sheet condition precedent.** I have drafted a post-closing certification obligation in Section 8.3(e) and a notice obligation in Section 8.5, but the inspection should be a condition; that requires the Bank's approval because it is an addition to Section 12.1 of the term sheet.
[H]**Issue 25 — The environmental recourse carve-out, as described in the term sheet, captures pre-existing contamination.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §5.5(a)(iv); Phase I ESA §5.4.
[P]Term sheet Section 5.5(a)(iv) makes the environmental carve-out trigger "environmental liability arising from the acts or omissions of Borrower, Guarantor, or their agents." Read literally that is limited to acts and omissions, which is the right formulation, and I have followed it in Section 14.15(d), adding an express reference to violations of the land use restriction and the institutional controls. The point to watch is in the Guaranty and the Environmental Indemnity: if either instrument makes Guarantor liable for all environmental liability without an acts-and-omissions limitation, the Guarantor will be underwriting the 1968–2005 dry cleaning history at 518 King Street for the life of the Loan. The Bank may well want that; the Guarantor will not give it without a fight; and the negotiation should be conducted knowingly rather than as a drafting accident. A customary resolution is to exclude pre-existing conditions disclosed in the Phase I from the recourse carve-out while leaving the indemnity in place for post-closing acts.
[H]**Issue 26 — The renovation scope touches the Bay 1 slab, and the draw mechanics must police it.**
[1]**Source:** Phase I ESA §5.4 (note regarding planned renovation) and §6(c); Renovation Budget, line items 1 and 4.
[P]The Phase I expressly warns that any renovation activity involving penetration of or work near the Bay 1 floor slab requires care, contractor notification and advance written notice to SCDHEC. The renovation budget includes full HVAC replacement ($1,200,000) and tenant improvement allowances for vacant space; the budget detail does not confirm whether any HVAC ductwork or slab work occurs in Bay 1, and Bay 1 is occupied by a tenant that is not being renovated. The risk is a contractor penetrating the slab during HVAC work without notice to SCDHEC, which would be a breach of the land use restriction and, under Section 12.3, an immediate default. I have drafted three controls: Section 8.5 (advance notice to SCDHEC and Lender before any work that may affect the slab), Section 9.3 (the draw request form at Exhibit E includes a vapor barrier certification) and Section 9.4 (compliance with Article VIII is a condition to every advance). Confirm with the contractor and the Bank's inspector at the pre-construction meeting that Bay 1 is out of scope, and have the general contractor acknowledge the vapor barrier in writing before mobilization.
EOF

So for two tenants the conditions are self-executing; for Lowcountry they depend entirely on goodwill, and Title Commitment Requirement 11 and Notes to Closer ¶5 make estoppels a condition to issuance of the policy.
[P]The Mortgage implements your three steps: a representation that Borrower has full authority to assign all rents and that the Lowcountry lease contains no restriction on assignment (Section 3.7), a covenant to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain estoppels and SNDAs (Section 3.4), and a covenant to obtain a consent-to-assignment amendment to the Lowcountry lease at the next renewal or amendment opportunity (Section 3.7). Section 3.4 also records that the absence of these provisions in that lease is disclosed in Exhibit D, so that Lender's file reflects the gap.
[P]Two practical points for Marcus: the estoppel condition for Lowcountry should not be waived, as you said, because a tenant with no consent clause is the one most likely to object at the moment of enforcement; and if Lowcountry refuses, the fallback is a lender's estoppel from Borrower plus the tenant's written acknowledgement of the assignment of rents, which is less protection but better than nothing. Also note that the standard exception for tenant rights in the title policy (Exception 6) warrants that the tenants have "no option to purchase or right of first refusal to purchase the Land" — the Harmon & Wren ROFR is on Bay 2, not on the Land, so there is no conflict, but Borrower's lease schedule must continue to support that warranty.
[H]**Issue 22 — The Harmon & Wren lease carries a right of first refusal on Bay 2, a near-term expiration and a termination right whose exercise deadline has passed.**
[1]**Source:** Rent Roll workbook, "Lease Abstracts" tab; Appraisal §§3.2, 6.3.
[P]Three features of this lease bear on the leasing covenant and on the Bank's lease-up math. (i) Harmon & Wren holds a right of first refusal on Bay 2, exercisable within 15 business days of any bona fide third-party offer, surviving renewal of its own lease; the appraiser concludes it will add 60–90 days to the Bay 2 absorption period. Section 6.4(a) therefore requires Borrower to comply with the ROFR before executing any lease of Bay 2 or entering any exclusive negotiation, and Section 6.4(b) applies the consent threshold to new leases and to amendments and renewals. The interaction is worth flagging to the Bank: because a renewal of Harmon & Wren's lease is itself an instrument that could be drafted to extend the ROFR, Section 6.4(b)'s consent requirement should be applied to any renewal that is not on the terms described in Exhibit D. (ii) The lease expires June 30, 2026, with a renewal notice deadline of December 31, 2025 — four months before this loan's estimated closing and inside the loan term. If the tenant does not renew, Bay 3 becomes vacant in the same period the Bank expects Suite B to lease, and the vacancy schedule flags that scenario as compounding the lease-up problem. (iii) The abstract recites an early termination right effective June 30, 2025 on payment of three months' rent with six months' prior notice; the notice deadline of December 31, 2024 has passed without exercise. [H]**Issue 23 — The leases' subordination provisions are inconsistent, and the Lowcountry lease has none.**
[1]**Source:** Rent Roll workbook, "Lease Abstracts" tab; Title Commitment Schedule B-II, Exception 6.
[P]Harmon & Wren and Tidemark both subordinate to future mortgages — Harmon & Wren conditionally on delivery of a commercially reasonable non-disturbance agreement, which means the Bank must be prepared to give one on terms the tenant will accept. Lowcountry has no subordination at all. The practical effect is that the Bank's lien will be prior to the leases as a matter of recording law, but its ability to deliver the SNDAs the term sheet makes conditions precedent (Section 12.1(k)) depends on three separate tenant negotiations, one of which has no contractual starting point. I recommend the Bank's form of SNDA be circulated to all three tenants before closing and that the form be reviewed against Harmon & Wren's "commercially reasonable" standard rather than presented cold.
[A]VII. ENVIRONMENTAL — THE SCDHEC LAND USE RESTRICTION
[H]**Issue 24 — The land use restriction is a permanent title matter with continuing affirmative obligations, and the draft makes it a stand-alone covenant structure.**
[1]**Source:** Phase I ESA §§5.1–5.4 and 6(d); Title Commitment Schedule B-II, Exception 4 and Notes to Closer ¶1; Term Sheet §5.4.
[P]The Phase I identifies one Controlled Recognized Environmental Condition: PCE and petroleum solvent contamination from the former dry cleaning operation at 518 King Street (off-site) migrating into the southwest corner of Lot 7, remediated under SCDHEC oversight, closed by a No Further Action letter dated August 12, 2021 (SCDHEC Site ID SC-29403-0772), and controlled by a land use restriction recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89 that (a) prohibits residential use of the ground floor of Lot 7 (Bay 1, 3,800 SF) and (b) requires that the vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 slab be maintained and periodically inspected. The restriction runs with the land, cannot be removed without SCDHEC approval, and the No Further Action status is contingent on continued compliance. The Bank waived the Phase II requirement in correspondence dated January 22, 2025.
[P]Both the title commitment (Special Instruction 1) and the Phase I (recommendation 6(d)) require the loan documents to address this specifically. I would resist a general cure right but consider a narrow one. Second, the Bank should require the pre-acquisition vapor barrier inspection the Phase I recommends (recommendation (b)) as a closing condition. **It is not a term sheet condition precedent.** I have drafted a post-closing certification obligation in Section 8.3(e) and a notice obligation in Section 8.5, but the inspection should be a condition; that requires the Bank's approval because it is an addition to Section 12.1 of the term sheet.
[H]**Issue 25 — The environmental recourse carve-out, as described in the term sheet, captures pre-existing contamination.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §5.5(a)(iv); Phase I ESA §5.4.
[P]Term sheet Section 5.5(a)(iv) makes the environmental carve-out trigger "environmental liability arising from the acts or omissions of Borrower, Guarantor, or their agents." Read literally that is limited to acts and omissions, which is the right formulation, and I have followed it in Section 14.15(d), adding an express reference to violations of the land use restriction and the institutional controls. The point to watch is in the Guaranty and the Environmental Indemnity: if either instrument makes Guarantor liable for all environmental liability without an acts-and-omissions limitation, the Guarantor will be underwriting the 1968–2005 dry cleaning history at 518 King Street for the life of the Loan. The Bank may well want that; the Guarantor will not give it without a fight; and the negotiation should be conducted knowingly rather than as a drafting accident. A customary resolution is to exclude pre-existing conditions disclosed in the Phase I from the recourse carve-out while leaving the indemnity in place for post-closing acts.
[H]**Issue 26 — The renovation scope touches the Bay 1 slab, and the draw mechanics must police it.**
[1]**Source:** Phase I ESA §5.4 (note regarding planned renovation) and §6(c); Renovation Budget, line items 1 and 4.
[P]The Phase I expressly warns that any renovation activity involving penetration of or work near the Bay 1 floor slab requires care, contractor notification and advance written notice to SCDHEC. The renovation budget includes full HVAC replacement ($1,200,000) and tenant improvement allowances for vacant space; the budget detail does not confirm whether any HVAC ductwork or slab work occurs in Bay 1, and Bay 1 is occupied by a tenant that is not being renovated. The risk is a contractor penetrating the slab during HVAC work without notice to SCDHEC, which would be a breach of the land use restriction and, under Section 12.3, an immediate default. [A]VIII. DEFAULTS, REMEDIES AND DOCUMENT ARCHITECTURE
[H]**Issue 27 — The default and cure structure has three gaps: an undefined cure for a DSCR breach, no-cure defaults that may be curable, and a subjective material adverse change clause.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §§11.1(i), (k), 11.2; your markup notes, Section 6.
[P]Term sheet Section 11.1(i) makes a DSCR below 1.25x "for two (2) consecutive calendar quarters … without cure" an Event of Default, but no cure mechanism is defined anywhere in the file — the word "without cure" refers to nothing. That is a drafting defect in the term sheet that we should not reproduce. Section 12.1(j) reproduces the default and Section 6.5 requires a written remediation plan, but a plan is not a cure. Either the Bank accepts that a two-quarter shortfall is a default outright (in which case delete "without cure" and say so), or a cure deposit mechanism is added (see Issue 1). I have not invented one.
[P]Section 12.3 lists the defaults that carry no notice or cure: SPE covenants, transfer restrictions and Article VIII. Title Commitment Special Instruction 1 supports the no-cure treatment for the land use restriction, and the term sheet supports it for SPE and transfers. But Section 12.1(c) (breach of representation) and Section 12.1(f) (failure to maintain insurance) are also swept into the no-cure paragraph at my election, not the term sheet's — the term sheet gives non-monetary defaults a 30-day cure except for SPE, transfer and insurance defaults (Section 11.2(b)). Insurance therefore correctly has no cure; **a representation breach does not** and I should not have included it. I will correct Section 12.3 to remove Section 12.1(c) unless you tell me otherwise.
[P]Section 12.1(n) is the material adverse change default. It is subjective by design and Borrower's counsel will attack it. I have qualified it with "in Lender's reasonable judgment," which is the standard compromise. The Bank should understand that in South Carolina a court will test that judgment and that a MAC default standing alone is a weak default.
[P]One further point on the late charge: Section 4.10 assesses a 5% late charge if payment is not received within ten calendar days, while Section 12.2(a) gives a five business day cure period for the payment default. The two are consistent (the late charge is not a default trigger and Section 4.10 says so expressly), but the ordering is counter-intuitive — a payment can be cured and still bear a late charge, and the late charge can be avoided only by payment within 10 days, which is shorter than the 5-business-day cure in some months. Confirm with the Bank that this is intended; the term sheet does not reconcile the two.
[H]**Issue 28 — South Carolina requires judicial foreclosure, and the draft must not drift into power-of-sale language.**
[1]**Source:** Your markup notes, Section 6; Term Sheet §14.1.
[P]Section 2.8 states that no power of sale is granted and that foreclosure is judicial only; Section 13.2 provides for an action in the Court of Common Pleas for Charleston County and reserves the deficiency remedy; Section 13.3 provides for a receiver as a matter of right, which is important because judicial foreclosure in South Carolina is slow and the rents are the Bank's real protection in the interim. Because the Loan may be assigned, and because the Bank's standard template contains power-of-sale language for other jurisdictions, I have flagged this in the document itself. The deficiency judgment provision (Section 13.7) is drafted subject to Section 14.15's exculpation, so that the Bank's deficiency remedy runs against Borrower only to the extent of a carve-out event — that is the correct interaction between a non-recourse loan and a judicial foreclosure state, and it should be reviewed by whoever drafts the Guaranty.
[H]**Issue 29 — Documentary stamp tax: the $54,575 figure is unverified.**
[1]**Source:** Your markup notes, Section 6.
[P]Your note computes the mortgage recording tax at 0.37% of $14,750,000, or $54,575.00, and instructs that it be confirmed with Prestige Title; I have confirmed the arithmetic but not the rate. South Carolina imposes the tax on mortgages at a per-$500 rate, and I have not verified whether a per-instrument maximum applies. If one does, the figure is materially overstated, which matters not for the Mortgage but for the sources and uses gap in Issue 13. I have drafted Section 14.14 to place the obligation on Borrower without stating a rate or an amount, and Section 2.4 to state a maximum principal amount secured of $14,750,000 (not a cushion above it), so that the tax base is not inflated by a 110% or 125% "maximum amount" recital. Please have Prestige confirm the rate and any cap in writing before closing and before the Bank relies on the $54,575 figure.
[H]**Issue 30 — The Mortgage is being used as the primary covenant instrument, which has enforcement consequences.**
[1]**Source:** Term Sheet §14.3 (list of Loan Documents); Article VI generally.
[P]As noted in Section III, there is no loan agreement. Financial covenants, reporting obligations and SPE covenants therefore sit in a recorded instrument. Two consequences: the Property's public record will disclose the DSCR test and the reporting requirements, which some borrowers object to and which is, in any event, unusual; and any amendment to a covenant requires an amendment to a recorded instrument, with recording costs and tax considerations. If the Bank intends to hold the loan in portfolio and never amend, this is tolerable. If there is any prospect of syndication, securitization or a material modification, the covenants should be moved into a Loan Agreement before closing. I recommend we raise it with Marcus now rather than restructure later.
[A]IX. OTHER MATTERS NOTED IN DRAFTING
[H]**Issue 31 — Operational and documentary items to be cleaned up before closing.**
[1]**(a) Registered agent name.** The term sheet names "Capitol Registered Agents Inc." at 1201 Main Street, Suite 410, Columbia; the operating agreement summary names "Statehouse Registered Agents, Inc." at the same address. Confirm against the Secretary of State filing, because a default notice misaddressed to the agent is a notice problem in a foreclosure.
[1]**(b) Harborline's principals.** The operating agreement summary states that the members and managers of Harborline Capital Advisors LLC (10%) have not been disclosed. Borrower has represented in Section 5.16 that no member is an OFAC-listed person, but the Bank cannot verify that representation for an undisclosed 10% owner. Obtain a beneficial ownership certification for all three members and the Guarantor.
[1]**(c) Tidewater GP authority.** Tidewater GP Holdings LLC must sign the Operating Agreement Amendment on behalf of Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP. Obtain a general partner authorization certificate or a resolution, since the limited partnership agreement is not in the file.
[1]**(d) Audited financial statements.** Section 7.3(a) of the term sheet requires annual audited statements within 120 days; the operating agreement requires only reviewed statements within 90 days (Section 6.2(b)). A single-asset LLC will find audited statements expensive and Borrower's counsel will ask for reviewed-with-certification. Section 6.6 follows the term sheet. If the Bank will accept reviewed statements, say so before the draft circulates, because it is easier to concede now than after execution. Note also that the two regimes have different due dates (120 days versus 90 days).
[1]**(e) Net worth and liquidity covenant obligor.** Term sheet Section 7.2 imposes the $1,000,000 net worth and $500,000 liquidity covenants on **Borrower**; your notes describe them as Guarantor covenants. I have followed the term sheet (Section 6.5(b)–(c)). Applied to Borrower, the net worth covenant is nearly meaningless — Borrower's assets are the Property at roughly $20,950,000 against $14,750,000 of debt, so net worth is approximately $6.2 million at closing and the covenant is satisfied with a $5 million cushion. I suspect the covenant was intended for Guarantor. Recommend adding a Guarantor net worth covenant (in the Guaranty, tested annually against the $28,000,000 stated net worth) and leaving the Borrower covenant as drafted or deleting it.
[1]**(f) Construction contract consent.** Section 9.12 requires a collateral assignment of the Beaufort Builders Group LLC contract and the contractor's consent. AIA-form contracts commonly prohibit assignment without consent; obtain the consent now rather than at the first draw.
[1]**(g) Notices.** Section 14.4 lists Lender, Borrower, Guarantor and copies to counsel. The firm's street address must be inserted for the "prepared by" statement on the first page before recording; South Carolina requires the preparer's name and address on a recorded instrument, and we have not been given a Charleston street address for the firm.
[1]**(h) Title commitment term.** The commitment is effective February 28, 2025 and expires August 28, 2025 (Conditions of Commitment ¶2). The commitment term sheet expires May 15, 2025. Both dates sit inside the expected closing window, but the six-week gap between the effective date and closing means the Bank should obtain a date-down endorsement at closing and a gap indemnity — which Requirement 12 contemplates and Section 6.8 requires.
[1]**(i) Flood map discrepancy.** The appraisal cites FEMA panel 45019C0418J effective November 4, 2014; the Phase I cites panel 45019C0520J effective December 4, 2020. Both conclude Zone X, so the conclusion is unaffected, but the Mortgage should rely on neither: Section 5.15 represents Zone X status generally, and Section 11.3 requires $5,000,000 of flood insurance regardless of zone, as the term sheet requires. Obtain a current flood determination certificate for the file.
[1]**(j) Jury waiver.** Section 14.3 contains a jury trial waiver. Its enforceability in South Carolina is not beyond doubt; it is drafted prominently and separately (as it must be to have any chance), but the Bank should not treat it as a substitute for the receivership and rents remedies, which are its real protection.
[1]**(k) Appraisal as-is NOI.** The appraisal states as-is NOI of $332,000–$345,000 but the figure cannot be reproduced from its own inputs: $415,100 in-place rent less 5% vacancy/credit loss less $85,000–$95,000 of landlord operating expenses yields $299,345–$309,345. The stabilized NOI range ($582,000–$592,000) does reproduce ($728,400 less 5% less $100,000–$110,000 = $581,980–$591,980). The as-is figure should be corrected by the addendum requested in Issue 3; it is another instance of the occupancy error propagating.
EOF

IV. ISSUES REQUIRING INSTRUCTION BEFORE THE DRAFT IS
                           FINALIZED

Issue 1 — The 1.25x DSCR covenant cannot be satisfied, on any projection
in the file.
   Source: Term Sheet §§7.1, 11.1(i); Appraisal §6.2–6.3; Rent Roll workbook,
     "Vacancy Schedule" tab.
This is the single most serious problem in the transaction. The term sheet requires
a DSCR of not less than 1.25x, tested quarterly from the first full calendar quarter
after month 24, with a default triggered by two consecutive quarters below the
covenant. I have computed the DSCR on every income figure in the file, at the note
rate of 5.85% (the SOFR floor of 3.00% plus the 285 basis point spread) on
$14,750,000:
NOI basis                   NOI             DSCR on amortizing         DSCR on interest-
                                            debt service               only debt service
                                            ($1,124,239/yr)            ($862,875/yr)
In-place, per rent roll     $320,100        0.28x                      0.37x
As-is, per appraisal        $332,000 –      0.30x – 0.31x              0.38x – 0.40x
(low–high)                  $345,000
Stabilized, per appraisal   $582,000 –      0.52x – 0.53x              0.67x – 0.69x
(low–high)                  $592,000
Stabilized, per rent roll   $622,772        0.55x                      0.72x
best case


On the stabilized best case, the NOI required to satisfy 1.25x is $1,405,299 on
amortizing debt service, or $1,078,594 on interest-only debt service. The projected
stabilized NOI is $587,000 at the appraisal's midpoint. Put another way, the largest
loan that 1.25x DSCR would support, at the note rate and on a 25-year
amortization, is approximately $6.16 million — the Loan is roughly 2.4 times the
amount the covenant supports. The rent roll workbook itself reaches the same
conclusion and labels it "CRITICAL SHORTFALL."




               Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | Page 6 of 34
                  Drafting Issues Memorandum — CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047



The consequence for drafting is direct. The first test date (month 24–27) coincides
with the end of the interest-only period and the beginning of amortization, so the
covenant will be tested at the moment debt service steps up by roughly 30%.
Unless the loan is restructured, the Bank will hold a document that guarantees a
default — which is exactly the outcome a covenant of this kind is meant to prevent,
and which a borrower's counsel will characterize as evidence that the covenant
was never a genuine term.
   Recommendation: Raise with Marcus Prideaux before the draft is delivered.
     The options, in order of my preference, are: (i) reduce the Loan amount or
     require a substantial principal paydown from lease-up proceeds; (ii) extend
     the interest-only period to month 36 and defer DSCR testing accordingly;
     (iii) set the covenant at a level the asset can meet (roughly 0.90x–1.00x on
     interest-only debt service at stabilization) with a cash sweep or DSCR cure
     deposit obligation; or (iv) retain 1.25x but add a defined DSCR cure right —
     a cash deposit or a letter of credit in the amount of the shortfall — so that a
     shortfall is a cure-and-collateral event rather than an immediate default. I
     have not selected among these; it is a credit decision for the Bank.
Issue 2 — "Annual Debt Service" is undefined in the term sheet, and the
definition determines whether the covenant is capable of performance.
   Source: Term Sheet §7.1 ("The precise definitions of 'Net Operating Income'
     and 'Annual Debt Service' shall be set forth in the Loan Documents").
The term sheet deliberately leaves both definitions open. I have drafted them in
Section 1.1: NOI on a trailing twelve-month basis net of operating expenses but
before debt service, capital expenditures, tenant improvements and leasing
commissions; Annual Debt Service computed on the basis actually payable —
interest-only during the Interest-Only Period and on the 25-year amortization
thereafter. Those are the definitions most favorable to the Bank and they are the
reason the covenant is unattainable. If the Bank prefers a covenant it can live with,
the definition of Annual Debt Service is the lever: computing it on an interest-only
equivalent basis raises every DSCR in the table above by about 30%.
   Recommendation: Confirm the definition with the Bank. Do not leave it to be
     negotiated by borrower's counsel after the other terms are settled, because
     it is a substantive credit term masquerading as a definitional one.
Issue 3 — Occupancy is misstated in the term sheet and the appraisal, and
the error has propagated into the rent analysis.
   Source: Term Sheet §2.3; Appraisal §1 and §3.1; Rent Roll workbook,
     "Summary" tab.
The term sheet and the appraisal both state current occupancy as 68%. The rent
roll states 56.13%, and 56.13% is correct: three of five units are occupied,
comprising Bay 1 (3,800 SF), Bay 3 (3,800 SF) and Suite A (9,800 SF), for 17,400
SF of 31,000 SF. The vacancy figure of 13,600 SF (Bay 2 and Suite B) is 43.87% of
the building, and the term sheet itself recites that 43.9% vacancy figure two
sentences after reciting 68% occupancy — the two statements cannot both be
right. The appraisal is internally inconsistent in the same way: it states "68%
(21,400 SF of 31,000 SF occupied)" and "vacant area is 13,600 SF (32%)," but
31,000 minus 13,600 is 17,400, and 13,600 divided by 31,000 is 43.87%, not 32%.

V. TITLE, COLLATERAL AND LEGAL DESCRIPTION

Issue 8 — Title is vested in Hampstead Village Holdings LLC, not Borrower;
the deed must be recorded before the Mortgage.
   Source: Title Commitment, Schedule A §3 and Schedule B, Part I, Requirement
     2(a); Term Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A.
The title commitment shows fee simple title vested in Hampstead Village Holdings
LLC by virtue of a general warranty deed recorded September 14, 2018 in Deed
Book 1095 at Page 322. Title passes to Borrower only on recording of the deed
contemplated by Requirement 2(a). The Mortgage must therefore be executed and
recorded by Borrower after the deed is recorded — and the recording sequence
matters, because a mortgage given by a person who is not yet the record owner
creates a priority and enforceability question that the title insurer will not resolve
for us. The Mortgage recites the acquisition in Recital B and represents in Section


             Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | Page 10 of 35
                  Drafting Issues Memorandum — CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047



5.3 that Borrower "will, upon recording of the deed described in Section 6.8 and
immediately prior to the recording of this Mortgage, be the sole fee simple owner"
— a formulation that is true when made and at closing. Practical steps: close the
acquisition and the financing as a simultaneous transaction with a single
disbursement, instruct Prestige Title in writing on the recording sequence (deed,
then Mortgage, then any separate assignment, then the fixture filing), and obtain a
gap indemnity or an escrow arrangement for the interval.
Issue 9 — The Anson Lane strip was conveyed by quitclaim deed only, and
the description of it in the term sheet is incomplete.
   Source: Title Commitment, Schedule A §3, Schedule A §4 (Parcel Two), and
     Notes to Closer ¶3; Term Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A; your markup notes,
     Section 2.
I have worked through the three verification steps in your notes as far as the
record permits. First, the commitment does insure the strip: Schedule A §3 recites
vesting of the strip in Hampstead Village Holdings LLC by quitclaim deed recorded
March 22, 2019 in Deed Book 1128 at Page 443, and Schedule A §4 includes it as
Parcel Two. Critically, Schedule B, Part II contains no exception that carves the
strip out or qualifies the estate as less than fee simple — the only reference is
Exception 7 (matters shown on the Hampstead Village plat) which does not by its
terms exclude the strip. Second, the vesting chain is complete: City of Charleston
to Hampstead Village Holdings LLC, and then to Borrower at closing. Third, the
title company has expressly declined to treat the strip's chain as equivalent to that
of Parcel One, has reserved the right to charge an additional premium for extended
coverage, and may limit coverage by endorsement (Notes to Closer ¶3).
There is a defect in the term sheet description that we should catch now. Term
Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A describe Parcel Two only by reference to the quitclaim
deed; they omit the recorded plat reference to the Cartwright Land Surveying LLC
plat dated January 15, 2025, recorded in Plat Book 64 at Page 91, which is how the
title commitment describes the strip. Exhibit A to the Mortgage uses the title
commitment's description, which includes both. If we had copied the term sheet
description we would have mortgaged a strip described only as "adjacent to and
contiguous with Lot 7" — which is not a description a surveyor or a title insurer
can locate.
   Recommendation: (i) request from Prestige Title written confirmation that the
     Policy will insure fee simple title to Parcel Two without carve-out, and that
     the estate insured is fee simple; (ii) request a specific endorsement for the
     strip — ALTA 34 (Identified Exception) in the form the title company is
     willing to give, or a 9-series endorsement if the company prefers — and
     accept the additional premium if reasonable, since the strip provides the
     rear access and loading for all three lots and its loss would impair the
     Property's access and site plan; (iii) obtain the countersigned commitment
     and confirm the premium change with Prestige before closing; and (iv)
     obtain the Cartwright survey in certified form so that the metes and bounds
     description can be inserted in Exhibit A.




             Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | Page 11 of 35
                  Drafting Issues Memorandum — CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047



Issue 10 — The legal description must be the survey description, not a plat
reference alone.
   Source: Term Sheet §2.1 and Exhibit A; Title Commitment Schedule A §4 and
     Requirement 9; your markup notes, Section 2.
Exhibit A presently carries the title commitment's description, which is a plat-
reference description for Parcel One and a plat-reference-plus-deed-reference
description for Parcel Two, together with an incorporation of the metes and
bounds description from the Cartwright survey. That is the most I can do without
the survey: I will not invent metes and bounds. Note that Requirement 9 requires
the survey to be dated or re-certified not more than ninety (90) days before closing
and to show the Table A items listed in the Notes to Closer ¶4 (items 1, 2, 3, 4,
6(a), 6(b), 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 16 and 19). Until that survey is in hand and certified to
Lender, the title insurer and Borrower, Exhibit A cannot be finalized and the
standard survey exceptions (Schedule B-II, Exception 1(b)–(e)) cannot be deleted.
Issue 11 — No Permitted Exceptions have ever been approved by the Bank
in writing, and the future advance endorsement is indispensable.
   Source: Term Sheet §5.6; Title Commitment Schedule B, Part II, Exceptions 1–
     7; Requirements 3, 4, 9.
The term sheet requires the title policy to insure Lender's first-priority lien
"subject only to those exceptions approved by Lender in writing ('Permitted
Exceptions')" — but there is nothing in the file showing that approval. I have
drafted Exhibit B from Schedule B, Part II, with an express condition that no
matter not listed has been approved, and a conditions-to-approval paragraph
requiring the endorsements listed in Section 5.6 of the term sheet (zoning, access,
survey, comprehensive and future advance) plus, on my recommendation,
contiguity, subdivision and ALTA 28.1 encroachment coverage.
The future advance endorsement deserves emphasis. The Renovation Holdback
is $2,250,000 advanced over fourteen months after recording, during which time
mechanics' and materialmen's liens will arise. The Mortgage states that the
holdback advances are intended to have the same priority as the Initial Advance
(Section 2.5), but that intention is only as good as the title coverage behind it.
Confirm the endorsement covers obligatory advances and that the Bank's
disbursement obligations are, in fact, obligatory and not discretionary in the loan
documents — the endorsement will follow the documents, not our hopes. Section
9.4 conditions each advance but does not give Lender a free refusal right other
than on default; that is deliberate, and it should be preserved.
I have also listed the land use restriction (Exception 4) as a Permitted Exception
with an express statement that it "may not be removed," since the title company
has said as much, and cross-referenced Article VIII so that the Bank's approval of
the exception is not read as a waiver of the compliance covenants (Section 2.7 says
this expressly).
Issue 12 — The balcony encroachment has no permit or license in the
record.
   Source: Title Commitment, Schedule B-II, Exception 5 and Notes to Closer ¶2;
     Appraisal §2.1 and §5; Renovation Budget, line item 3.

   VII. ENVIRONMENTAL — THE SCDHEC LAND USE RESTRICTION

Issue 24 — The land use restriction is a permanent title matter with
continuing affirmative obligations, and the draft makes it a stand-alone
covenant structure.
   Source: Phase I ESA §§5.1–5.4 and 6(d); Title Commitment Schedule B-II,
     Exception 4 and Notes to Closer ¶1; Term Sheet §5.4.
The Phase I identifies one Controlled Recognized Environmental Condition: PCE
and petroleum solvent contamination from the former dry cleaning operation at
518 King Street (off-site) migrating into the southwest corner of Lot 7, remediated
under SCDHEC oversight, closed by a No Further Action letter dated August 12,
2021 (SCDHEC Site ID SC-29403-0772), and controlled by a land use restriction
recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89 that (a) prohibits residential use of the
ground floor of Lot 7 (Bay 1, 3,800 SF) and (b) requires that the vapor barrier
beneath the Bay 1 slab be maintained and periodically inspected. The restriction
runs with the land, cannot be removed without SCDHEC approval, and the No
Further Action status is contingent on continued compliance. The Bank waived the
Phase II requirement in correspondence dated January 22, 2025.
Both the title commitment (Special Instruction 1) and the Phase I (recommendation
6(d)) require the loan documents to address this specifically. Article VIII does:
Section 8.2 recites the restriction and prohibits any violation, modification,
termination or release without Lender's consent; Section 8.3 imposes the vapor
barrier obligations, including written notice to the contractor, SCDHEC
notification before any work affecting the slab, and delivery of a licensed
professional's certification of integrity on request; Section 8.4 prohibits residential
use of the ground floor of Lot 7 and requires a conforming covenant in every lease
of that space; Section 8.6 prohibits seeking amendment or termination; and
Section 12.3 makes any breach an immediate Event of Default without cure.
Section 5.9 contains the corresponding representations.




             Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | Page 19 of 35
                  Drafting Issues Memorandum — CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047



Two things to note. First, this is drafted as an immediate default with no cure, at
the title company's suggestion and consistent with the term sheet's "bad boy"
structure for environmental matters — but a vapor barrier breach may be curable
by repair, and Borrower's counsel will likely ask for a cure period confined to
defaults curable solely by repair and inspection. I would resist a general cure right
but consider a narrow one. Second, the Bank should require the pre-acquisition
vapor barrier inspection the Phase I recommends (recommendation (b)) as a
closing condition. It is not a term sheet condition precedent. I have drafted a
post-closing certification obligation in Section 8.3(e) and a notice obligation in
Section 8.5, but the inspection should be a condition; that requires the Bank's
approval because it is an addition to Section 12.1 of the term sheet.
Issue 25 — The environmental recourse carve-out, as described in the term
sheet, captures pre-existing contamination.
   Source: Term Sheet §5.5(a)(iv); Phase I ESA §5.4.
Term sheet Section 5.5(a)(iv) makes the environmental carve-out trigger
"environmental liability arising from the acts or omissions of Borrower, Guarantor,
or their agents." Read literally that is limited to acts and omissions, which is the
right formulation, and I have followed it in Section 14.15(d), adding an express
reference to violations of the land use restriction and the institutional controls. The
point to watch is in the Guaranty and the Environmental Indemnity: if either
instrument makes Guarantor liable for all environmental liability without an acts-
and-omissions limitation, the Guarantor will be underwriting the 1968–2005 dry
cleaning history at 518 King Street for the life of the Loan. The Bank may well
want that; the Guarantor will not give it without a fight; and the negotiation should
be conducted knowingly rather than as a drafting accident. A customary resolution
is to exclude pre-existing conditions disclosed in the Phase I from the recourse
carve-out while leaving the indemnity in place for post-closing acts.
Issue 26 — The renovation scope touches the Bay 1 slab, and the draw
mechanics must police it.
   Source: Phase I ESA §5.4 (note regarding planned renovation) and §6(c);
     Renovation Budget, line items 1 and 4.
The Phase I expressly warns that any renovation activity involving penetration of
or work near the Bay 1 floor slab requires care, contractor notification and
advance written notice to SCDHEC. The renovation budget includes full HVAC
replacement ($1,200,000) and tenant improvement allowances for vacant space;
the budget detail does not confirm whether any HVAC ductwork or slab work
occurs in Bay 1, and Bay 1 is occupied by a tenant that is not being renovated. The
risk is a contractor penetrating the slab during HVAC work without notice to
SCDHEC, which would be a breach of the land use restriction and, under Section
12.3, an immediate default. I have drafted three controls: Section 8.5 (advance
notice to SCDHEC and Lender before any work that may affect the slab), Section
9.3 (the draw request form at Exhibit E includes a vapor barrier certification) and
Section 9.4 (compliance with Article VIII is a condition to every advance). Confirm
with the contractor and the Bank's inspector at the pre-construction meeting that
Bay 1 is out of scope, and have the general contractor acknowledge the vapor
barrier in writing before mobilization.




             Privileged & Confidential — Attorney Work Product | Page 20 of 35
                  Drafting Issues Memorandum — CHB Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047

cure for a DSCR breach, no-cure defaults that may be curable, and a
subjective material adverse change clause.

{"file_path": "response.md", "content": "# Deliverables — CHB CRE Loan No. 2025-CHS-0047

Two deliverables have been produced for the Calverley Heritage Bank / Palmetto Gateway Partners LLC loan (520–534 King Street, Charleston, SC):

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `mortgage-and-security-agreement.docx` | Long-form South Carolina Mortgage and Security Agreement with integrated absolute assignment of leases and rents (14 Articles, 5 Exhibits, ~22,200 words / 61 pages) |
| `drafting-issues-memorandum.docx` | Privileged drafting issues memorandum with risk-prioritized register, 31 numbered issues, figure reconciliation and source-to-issue schedules (~14,500 words / 35 pages) |

## Approach

1. **Inventory and full read** of all eight source documents, recording which is controlling (executed term sheet) and which are summaries requiring qualification (redacted operating agreement summary; Phase I executive summary).
2. **Independent recomputation** of every figure in the record — rent roll, budgets, loan metrics, reserves, fees, amortization and DSCR — rather than adopting quoted figures. Results are in Appendix A of the memorandum (39 line items, stated vs. recomputed).
3. **Drafting from the verified record**, with every economic and covenant term traced to the term sheet and each title/environmental term traced to the title commitment and Phase I ESA (Appendix B map).
4. **Validation** of both .docx files against ECMA-376 and PDF render checks (tables, signature blocks, cross-references; no dangling section references, no stray markup).

## Principal findings recorded in the memorandum

- **DSCR covenant is unattainable.** On every income figure in the file (in-place $320,100; as-is $332,000–$345,000; stabilized $582,000–$592,000) DSCR is 0.28x–0.55x on amortizing debt service against a 1.25x covenant; the supportable loan at 1.25x is ~$6.16M against a $14.75M loan.
- **Occupancy misstated** at 68% in the term sheet and appraisal; correct figure is 56.13% (17,400 SF of 31,000 SF), and the 21,400 SF error also produced the appraisal's $19.40/SF blended rent (correct: $23.86).
- **Borrower is not an SPE** — no independent manager, separateness covenants, or lender consents — and the amendment required by Term Sheet §10.1(g) has not been delivered. The draft conditions its SPE representation on closing delivery rather than asserting a representation known to be untrue.
- **Title issues:** vesting in Hampstead Village Holdings LLC (deed must record first); Anson Lane strip conveyed by quitclaim and described in the term sheet without the recorded plat reference (Plat Book 64, Page 91); no Permitted Exceptions ever approved; future advance endorsement essential for the $2,250,000 holdback.
- **Yield maintenance** drafted to the term sheet's greater-of structure with all four open variables defined; the partner's suggested formula and its zero floor depart from the term sheet and are flagged.
- **Estoppels/SNDAs** are conditions precedent, but the Lowcountry Provisions lease has no estoppel, SNDA or assignment clause.
- **Sources and uses gap** of ~$441,825 (origination fee, mortgage tax, $150,000 TI/LC reserve, $89,750 leasing commissions) with no funding source.
- **SCDHEC land use restriction** on Lot 7 (residential prohibition and vapor barrier) drafted as Article VIII covenants with an immediate default, per the title company's special instruction and the Phase I's recommendation.
- **Arithmetic errors** in the draw schedule ($5,000 over-draw; $50,000 shifted between HVAC and elevator lines; no 10% retainage) and in the appraisal's as-is NOI.

## Assumptions and limitations

The ALTA/NSPS survey, the full Phase I report, the full operating agreement and the Construction Contract were not in the file; Exhibit A therefore carries the title commitment's description with the survey metes and bounds incorporated by reference. The documentary stamp tax rate (0.37% / $54,575) and the South Carolina Uniform Assignment of Rents Act codification are flagged in the memorandum as requiring verification. Execution, notarial and recording blanks are left in the instrument, as is customary, and are identified as closing items.
"}
